newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: U.S. ties with Japan, China better - Kantor.
newsitem.headline: U.S. ties with Japan, China better - Kantor.

text.p: U.S. ties with Japan and China are improving as President Bill Clinton heads towards meetings with his Japanese and Chinese counterparts this weekend, U.S. Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor said on Saturday.
"Our relations with China are much stronger than they were just a few months ago," Kantor told Reuters Financial Television, referring to tensions in the Taiwan Strait earlier this year.
Clinton will meet Chinese President Jiang Zemin and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Sunday on the fringes of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference here.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher prepared the way for the Chinese meeting on a visit to Beijing this week, his first since 1994, when ties hit a low point over China's human rights record.
Christopher soft-pedalled human rights issues during the visit, but won China's reaffirmation to curb missile sales and adopt nationwide export controls.

"There is no such thing as softening or hardening our stance. We believe in full and complete engagement with China," he added in the interview, which covered issues ranging from human rights, Chinese missile sales abroad and trade disputes.
He said the United States is actively working to get China accepted into the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
"As far as the WTO is concerned, it is the U.S. that is most active, not only in supporting China's accession, but working with China to achieve that accession," Kantor said.
"We're not the only country. Most other countries, in fact, say it should be done on a commercially reasonable basis. However, within that, we are being practical, pragmatic, flexible and realistic."
China has applied to join the WTO on favourable terms given to developing countries, but Washington insists that China's economy is too big for this treatment.
U.S. officials say "commercially meaningful terms" means that China has to go much further in opening up its markets as well as abide by WTO rules and processes.

Clinton will likely focus on trade issues in his talks with Jiang. China, for its part, wants Washington to back its application to join the World Trade Organisation, which holds its inaugural ministerial meeting in Singapore next month.
The United States said on Wednesday its trade deficit with China climbed to nearly $29 billion in the first nine months of the year, from $25 billion in the same period last year.
Kantor said Washington was concerned about the deficit because it was not based on macroeconomic factors "but a product of unfair discrimination".
"For instance, China unfortunately has implemented quotas, licenses and other arrangements...which have adversely affected U.S. exports to China."
Kantor was also sanguine about progress on trade issues with Japan, saying newly re-elected Japanese Prime Minister Hashimoto has said he is committed to deregulation and structural reform.
"I predict we'll make some progress over the next few months," he said.

But he was less than pleased with progress on Washington's chronic dispute over Japanese market penetration for U.S. car firms. He said Japan could do better about expanding the number of American auto dealerships in Japan.
"I think we could do better. We've had 122 new dealerships since the last agreement went into effect. We expected 200 by the end of the year. We're not going to meet that goal."
He said the United States would remain firm when it resumes talks in Tokyo next week about Japanese deregulation of its insurance industry.
